claim: 6 months-old memories in mice roughly correspond to 20 year-old memory traces in humans based on life expectancy.
source: we imaged brain activity in mice during retrieval of recent, early remote and very remote fear memories by detecting the immediate-early gene Arc. Investigating correlates of the memory trace over an extended period allowed us to report that, in contrast to CA1, CA3 is no longer recruited in very remote retrieval.
evidence: The manuscript states that 6 months and 1 year-old memories in mice correspond to 20 and 40 year-old memories in humans based on life expectancy calculations.

claim: 1 year-old memories in mice roughly correspond to 40 year-old memory traces in humans based on life expectancy.
source: To identify the specific role of these areas, we imaged brain activity in mice during retrieval of recent, early remote and very remote fear memories by detecting the immediate-early gene Arc.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this correspondence based on life expectancy calculations.

claim: CA3 is no longer recruited in very remote memory retrieval.
source: Investigating correlates of the memory trace over an extended period allowed us to report that, in contrast to CA1, CA3 is no longer recruited in very remote retrieval.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Parahippocampal areas are maximally engaged during very remote memory retrieval.
source: Conversely, we showed that parahippocampal areas are then maximally engaged.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by Arc expression data.

claim: There is a shift from greater contribution of the trisynaptic loop to the temporoammonic pathway for retrieval of very remote memories.
source: These results suggest a shift from a greater contribution of the trisynaptic loop to the temporoammonic pathway for retrieval.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented, based on the differential engagement of CA3 and CA1 over time.

claim: According to system consolidation theory, memory becomes hippocampal-independent as it ages and is ultimately stored in the cortex.
source: Some studies showing temporally-graded retrograde amnesia following hippocampal damage in humans have provided evidence that memory becomes hippocampal-independent as it ages and is ultimately 'stored' in the cortex (Alvarez and Squire, 1994: "the system consolidation theory").
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Alvarez and Squire, 1994.

claim: According to multiple trace theory, the hippocampus supports cortical areas in retrieving more remote memories.
source: An alternative theory posits that the hippocampus is not only engaged in retrieving recent memories but that it also supports cortical areas in retrieving more remote memories (Nadel and Moscovitch, 1997: the 'multiple trace theory').
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nadel and Moscovitch, 1997.

claim: CA1 participates in the retrieval of early and very remote memories over 30 years-old in humans.
source: A recent lesion study in humans indicates that CA1 participates to the retrieval of early and very remote memories (over 30 years-old) in addition to its well-established role for recent memories (Bartsch et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bartsch et al., 2011.

claim: The role of CA3 in the retrieval of remote memory has rarely been investigated in animals for memories older than a month.
source: In contrast, the role of CA3 in the retrieval of remote memory has not been yet studied in humans and has rarely been investigated in animals for memories older than a month, a period of time roughly equivalent to four years in humans based on life expectancy.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: One month in mice is roughly equivalent to four years in humans based on life expectancy.
source: In contrast, the role of CA3 in the retrieval of remote memory has not been yet studied in humans and has rarely been investigated in animals for memories older than a month, a period of time roughly equivalent to four years in humans based on life expectancy.
evidence: This is a calculation based on life expectancy comparisons.

claim: CA3 contributes to retrieving memories via pattern completion processes.
source: Nonetheless, computational studies suggest that CA3 would contribute to retrieving memories, at least recent and early remote memory, via processes involving the completion of memory representations based on partial or degraded features of these representations (the 'pattern completion' theory: Rolls et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rolls et al., 1997.

claim: Memory for single features and details that could serve as retrieval cues degrades over time.
source: However, the memory for single features and/or details that could serve as retrieval cues degrades over time (Wiltgen and Silva, 2007; Wiltgen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wiltgen and Silva, 2007 and Wiltgen et al., 2010.

claim: All shocked groups showed stronger freezing than their no-shock controls at test.
source: All shocked groups showed stronger freezing than their no-shock controls at test as shown by differences in freezing levels significantly higher than 0 (a 55.9 ± 3.4% increase in average).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Freezing levels were similar across delays, suggesting that memory strength did not significantly differ as memory aged.
source: Importantly, freezing levels were similar across delays, suggesting that memory strength did not significantly differ as memory aged.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Conditioned mice reexposed to the conditioning chamber froze in average 36 ± 4.7% more than the conditioned mice tested in the new context.
source: Conditioned mice reexposed to the conditioning chamber froze in average 36 ± 4.7% more than the conditioned mice tested in the new context, demonstrating that the freezing levels were specific to the conditioning chamber.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The freezing behavior was specific to the conditioning context.
source: Conditioned mice reexposed to the conditioning chamber froze in average 36 ± 4.7% more than the conditioned mice tested in the new context, demonstrating that the freezing levels were specific to the conditioning chamber.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data comparing freezing in conditioning context vs. new context.

claim: CA1 is engaged independently of the age of the memory trace.
source: CA1 is engaged independently of the age of the memory trace while (D,E) activity levels in CA3 are negligible for very remote memories.
evidence: This is supported by Arc expression data shown in Figure 2B-C and Figure 3A.

claim: Activity levels in CA3 are negligible for very remote memories.
source: CA1 is engaged independently of the age of the memory trace while (D,E) activity levels in CA3 are negligible for very remote memories.
evidence: This is supported by Arc expression data shown in Figure 2D-E and Figure 3A.

claim: Parahippocampal areas are maximally engaged during the retrieval of very remote memories.
source: The parahippocampal areas, for example the LEC, are maximally engaged during the retrieval of very remote memories.
evidence: This is supported by Arc expression data shown in Figure 2F-G and Figure 5.

claim: Freezing levels upon re-exposure to the conditioning context were high and did not significantly differ between delays.
source: Freezing levels upon re-exposure to the conditioning context were high and did not significantly differ between delays, indicating that the memory for the footshock/context association was strong and that its strength was comparable between delays whether the memory was recent or remote (comparisons to 0: all ps<0.015, in average a 55.9 ± 3.4% increase in freezing compared to age-matched 'no-shock' groups; F(4,15) =0.26, p=0.897; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Memory strength was comparable between delays whether the memory was recent or remote.
source: Freezing levels upon re-exposure to the conditioning context were high and did not significantly differ between delays, indicating that the memory for the footshock/context association was strong and that its strength was comparable between delays whether the memory was recent or remote (comparisons to 0: all ps<0.015, in average a 55.9 ± 3.4% increase in freezing compared to age-matched 'no-shock' groups; F(4,15) =0.26, p=0.897; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: A difference in memory strength across delays cannot account for the differences in the pattern of activation reported in the present study.
source: Importantly, this result shows that a difference in memory strength across delays cannot account for the differences in the pattern of activation reported in the present study.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data showing comparable memory strength across delays.

claim: Freezing levels were strikingly lower when mice were exposed to a new context compared to the conditioning chamber.
source: In this case, freezing levels were strikingly lower than those observed by re-exposing the mice to the conditioning chamber, demonstrating that the freezing behavior was indeed specific to the conditioning context (one day: conditioning context: 52.4 ± 2.5% vs new context: 19.8 ± 5.9%; one year: conditioning context: 62.5 ± 8.4% vs new context: 21.9 ± 8.385%; both ts>3.9 and ps<0.007; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing contexts.

claim: CA3 was no longer engaged for memory retrieval at 6 months and 1 year time points.
source: Indeed, CA3 was no longer engaged for memory retrieval at this time point (F(4,15)=26.73, p<0.001; Tukey posthoc: recent or early remote traces vs very remote traces: all ps<0.028; comparisons to 0: up to 1 month-old traces: ps<0.010, 6 months and 1 year old traces: n.s).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of Arc expression data in CA3.

claim: CA1 was engaged for all delays and overall more activated than CA3.
source: Importantly, this was only the case for CA3 as revealed by a significant region by delay interaction and further statistical analysis showing that, in contrast to CA3, CA1 was engaged for all delays and overall more activated than CA3 (CA1 and CA3 comparisons to 0: all ps<0.033; area effect: F(1,30)=62.74, p<0.001; delay effect: F(4,30)=20.15, p<0.001; region by delay interaction effect: F(4,30)=5.84, p=0.001; post-hoc analysis: CA1 vs CA3: all ts>3.89 and ps<0.030 but for 6 months t=2.36, p=0.099 and 1 week n.s; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of Arc expression data comparing CA1 and CA3.

claim: Activation levels in CA1 were higher one day after conditioning compared to all other delays.
source: In addition, within-area analysis showed that activation levels in CA1 were higher one day after conditioning compared to all other delays but comparable between the remaining delays (F(4,15) = 9.46, p=0.001; Tukey posthoc: one day higher than any other delay: all ps<0.041 but for 1 month p=0.090; one week to one year: all ps>0.083 but 1 month vs 6 months: p=0.038).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of Arc expression data in CA1.

claim: Correlations between memory performance and Arc levels in CA3 were significant for recent and early remote memories but not for very remote memory traces.
source: This new finding of a time-limited involvement of CA3 for the retrieval of memory was further supported by significant correlations between memory performance and Arc levels in CA3 for recent and early remote memories, which failed to reach significant for very remote memory traces (recent and early remote: R2=0.47, p<0.001; very remote: R2=0.06, p=0.351; Figure 3B–C)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Correlations between memory performance and Arc levels in CA1 were significant independently of the age of the memory trace.
source: while correlations were significant for CA1 independently to the age of the memory trace (R2s.>0.40, ps<0.008; Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: Levels of activation in CA3 did not differ between the memory-impaired and the memory-intact animals that were tested one year after conditioning.
source: The lack of involvement of CA3 in the retrieval of very remote memories was further strengthened by the fact that levels of activation in CA3 did not differ between the memory-impaired and the memory-intact animals that were tested one year after conditioning (intact vs impaired: freezing index: t(6) = 4.32, p=0.005, Arc expression: t(6)=1.08, p=0.321, comparison to 0: n.s; see Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing memory-intact and memory-impaired groups.

claim: CA1 was not recruited in the memory-impaired group as opposed to the memory-intact group.
source: In a striking contrast and supporting a crucial role of CA1 in the retrieval of very remote memories, CA1 was not recruited in the memory-impaired group as opposed to the memory–intact group (intact vs impaired: t(6)=3.38, p=0.015; comparisons to 0: memory impaired: t(3)=0.08, p=0.936; memory intact: t(3)=6.69, p=0.007; see Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing memory-intact and memory-impaired groups.

claim: Baseline Arc expression was comparable between and within CA1 and CA3 over time.
source: Of note, these results are unlikely due to an age- related decline specific to CA3 since baseline Arc expression was comparable between and within CA1 and CA3 over time as shown by the absence of significant 'area' x 'delay' interaction, main area effects and posthocs analysis over time failing to reach significance (area effect: (F(1,30)= 2.30; p=0.14), delay effect: F(4,30)=0.77;p=0.55, area by delay interaction effect: (F(4,30)=40; p=0.81; posthocs: delay effects: CA1: F(4,20)= 0.63, p=0.65; CA3: F(4,20)=0.52, p=0.72)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of baseline Arc expression in home-cage controls.

claim: Arc expression elicited by a maximal electroconvulsive shock does not significantly differ between CA1 and CA3.
source: and because Arc expression elicited by a maximal electroconvulsive shock, a standard positive control for this type of study, does not significantly differ between CA1 and CA3 (Nakamura et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2013.

claim: The decline of Arc expression seen in CA3 is specific to the task.
source: Thus, these findings suggest that the decline of expression seen in CA3 is specific to the task.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of age-related decline in baseline Arc expression.

claim: There is a clear functional segregation of CA3 and CA1 in the retrieval of memory over time.
source: These results show for the first time a clear functional segregation of CA3 and CA1 in the retrieval of memory over time, with CA3 contributing only to the retrieval of recent and early remote memories and CA1 being recruited independently of the age of the memory trace.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the Arc expression data presented.

claim: All parahippocampal areas participated qualitatively to a comparable extent to retrieving memory over time as they were all maximally engaged for the retrieval of the oldest traces.
source: All parahippocampal areas participated qualitatively to a comparable extent to retrieving memory over time as they were all maximally engaged for the retrieval of the oldest traces.
evidence: This is supported by Arc expression data in parahippocampal areas.

claim: The PER and the LEC were more recruited than the POR and the MEC specifically for the oldest memory traces.
source: In addition, the PER and the LEC were more recruited than the POR and the MEC specifically for the oldest memory traces (PER vs LEC, PER vs POR, POR vs MEC and LEC vs MEC: delay effects: Fs(4,30)>18.89, ps<0.001; within-area analysis; LEC, PER and POR: all Fs(4,15)>6.69, ps<0.003; tukey posthocs: recent or early remote memories versus very remote memories: all ps<0.006; MEC: all ps<0.047 but for 1 month vs. 1 year: n.s; area effects: PER vs POR and LEC vs MEC: Fs(1,30)>10.91, ps<0.002; comparisons for 6 months and one year: ts(3)>3.77; ps<0.034 while PER vs LEC and POR vs MEC: n.s; interactions effects: PER vs POR and LEC vs MEC: Fs(4,30)>2.78, ps<0.045 while PER vs LEC and POR vs MEC: n.s).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of Arc expression data in parahippocampal areas.

claim: All parahippocampal areas were activated across all delays except the MEC and the POR for recent memories and the PER one week after conditioning.
source: In addition, all areas were activated across all delays (comparisons to 0: all ts>3.52, ps<0.039; Figure 5A, B) at the exception of the MEC and the POR for recent memories and the PER one week after conditioning (all ts<2.22, ps>0.113).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of Arc expression data in parahippocampal areas.

claim: Parahippocampal areas of animals showing impaired memory when tested one year after conditioning were significantly activated, albeit less than those of animals whose memory was intact.
source: Interestingly, parahippocampal areas of animals showing impaired memory when tested one year after conditioning were also significantly activated (see Figure 4C), albeit less than those of animals whose memory was intact (comparisons to 0: memory intact: ts(3)>3.821, ps<0.032; memory impaired: ts(3)>3.929, ps<0.029, except MEC: t(3)=2.65, p=0.077; intact vs. impaired: LEC and PER: ts(6)>5.58, ps<0.001; POR: t(6)= 2.27, p=0.063; MEC: t(6)=1.67, p=0.146).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing memory-intact and memory-impaired groups.

claim: A partial memory representation had been consolidated and stored in the cortical areas in the memory-impaired group, but weak activation of these areas alone does not suffice for successful retrieval.
source: This result might suggest that, in the memory-impaired group, a partial memory representation had been consolidated and stored in the cortical areas, but that a weak activation of these areas alone does not suffice for successful retrieval.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data from memory-impaired animals.

claim: The PER and LEC receive stronger connections from the amygdala than the MEC and the POR.
source: However, the PER and LEC, which receive stronger connections from the amygdala than the MEC and the POR, were more activated than the MEC and the POR during the retrieval of the most remote memories (6 months- and one-year old traces), a time point which coincides with the epoch at which cortical areas are thought to play a strong role in the retrieval of memories.
evidence: This is based on known anatomical connectivity patterns.

claim: The PER and LEC were more activated than the MEC and POR during the retrieval of very remote memories.
source: However, the PER and LEC, which receive stronger connections from the amygdala than the MEC and the POR, were more activated than the MEC and the POR during the retrieval of the most remote memories (6 months- and one-year old traces), a time point which coincides with the epoch at which cortical areas are thought to play a strong role in the retrieval of memories.
evidence: This is supported by Arc expression data in parahippocampal areas.

claim: The differential activation of PER/LEC vs MEC/POR suggests a segregation of the parahippocampal areas in terms of memory processes rather than in terms of spatial or non-spatial information processing.
source: This result suggests a segregation of the parahippocampal areas in terms of memory processes rather than in terms of spatial or non-spatial information processing at this time point.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential activation patterns observed.

claim: CA1 plays a critical role in the retrieval of very remote memories as activation of the parahippocampal areas alone appeared not to be sufficient for successful retrieval.
source: In addition, these results further underline the critical role of CA1 in the retrieval of very remote memories as activation of the parahippocampal areas alone appeared not to be sufficient for a successful retrieval of the memory trace at this time point.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of memory-intact and memory-impaired animals.

claim: Activity in the hippocampus was higher than that of the parahippocampal region for the retrieval of recent and early remote memories.
source: Activity in the hippocampus was higher than that of the parahippocampal region for the retrieval of recent and early remote memories while an inversed relationship emerged for the retrieval of very remote memories (area effect: F(1,30)=9.984; p=0.004; delay effect: F(4,30)=1.539; p=0.216; delay x area interaction effect: F(4,30)=61.629, p<0.001; post-hoc analysis: recent and early remote memory: ts>4.21, ps<0.024; very remote memories: ts>6.07 ps<0.009).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of averaged hippocampal and parahippocampal Arc expression.

claim: An inversed relationship emerged for the retrieval of very remote memories, with the parahippocampal region being more active than the hippocampus.
source: Activity in the hippocampus was higher than that of the parahippocampal region for the retrieval of recent and early remote memories while an inversed relationship emerged for the retrieval of very remote memories (area effect: F(1,30)=9.984; p=0.004; delay effect: F(4,30)=1.539; p=0.216; delay x area interaction effect: F(4,30)=61.629, p<0.001; post-hoc analysis: recent and early remote memory: ts>4.21, ps<0.024; very remote memories: ts>6.07 ps<0.009).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of averaged hippocampal and parahippocampal Arc expression.

claim: The hippocampus was significantly recruited independently of the age of the memory trace, even when CA1 and CA3 contributions were not dissociated.
source: Importantly, even under this condition, e.g. when the contribution of CA1 was not dissociated from that of CA3, the hippocampus was significantly recruited independently of the age of the memory trace (comparisons to 0: all ts>3.54 ps<0.038) in line with the multiple trace theory.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of averaged hippocampal Arc expression.

claim: If CA1 and CA3's contribution are not dissociated, the hippocampal contribution to the retrieval of very remote memories might be largely underestimated.
source: In conclusion, this analysis underlines the fact that, if CA1 and CA3's contribution are not dissociated, the hippocampal contribution to the retrieval of very remote memories might be largely underestimated.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing analyses with and without CA1/CA3 dissociation.

claim: The over-time shift from an engagement of the hippocampus to that of an engagement of the parahippocampal region in retrieving memory is only relative and not absolute.
source: Nevertheless, even in this case, the over-time shift from an engagement of the hippocampus to that of an engagement of the parahippocampal region in retrieving memory is only relative and not absolute, given that the hippocampus is still significantly activated even for the retrieval of very remote memories.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing continued hippocampal activation.

claim: This is the first evidence of a time-limited contribution of CA3 to the retrieval of memory.
source: Investigating memory retrieval over such an extended period of time enabled us to provide the first evidence of a time-limited contribution of CA3 to the retrieval of memory while, in striking contrast, CA1 remained involved regardless of the age of the memory trace.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: CA1 remained involved in memory retrieval regardless of the age of the memory trace.
source: Investigating memory retrieval over such an extended period of time enabled us to provide the first evidence of a time-limited contribution of CA3 to the retrieval of memory while, in striking contrast, CA1 remained involved regardless of the age of the memory trace.
evidence: This is supported by Arc expression data in CA1 across all time points.

claim: Parahippocampal areas were substantially more involved in retrieving very remote memory traces than more recent ones.
source: In addition, parahippocampal areas were substantially more involved in retrieving very remote memory traces than more recent ones and their activity patterns appeared to reflect memory demands rather than information content.
evidence: This is supported by Arc expression data in parahippocampal areas.

claim: Parahippocampal area activity patterns appeared to reflect memory demands rather than information content.
source: In addition, parahippocampal areas were substantially more involved in retrieving very remote memory traces than more recent ones and their activity patterns appeared to reflect memory demands rather than information content.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential activation of PER/LEC vs MEC/POR.

claim: No study has investigated the role of CA3 in retrieving remote memory traces in humans.
source: To our knowledge, no study has investigated the role of CA3 in retrieving remote memory traces in humans and only one studied early remote memory in animals (e.g. up to one month-old traces which roughly corresponds to a 4 year-old memory trace in humans based on life expectancy; Gusev et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: Only one study investigated CA3's role in early remote memory in animals.
source: To our knowledge, no study has investigated the role of CA3 in retrieving remote memory traces in humans and only one studied early remote memory in animals (e.g. up to one month-old traces which roughly corresponds to a 4 year-old memory trace in humans based on life expectancy; Gusev et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gusev et al., 2005.

claim: The lack of engagement of CA3 in retrieving very remote memories might stem from a failure to pattern complete memory representations.
source: However, since computational studies and studies that have limited their investigations to recent and early remote memory traces have speculated that CA3's contribution to memory retrieval would increase as memory ages because of an increasing demand on the completion of representations using partial or degraded features of these stored representations (the 'pattern completion theory': Rolls et al., 1997), we speculate that the lack of engagement of CA3 in retrieving very remote memories stems from a failure to 'pattern complete' memory representations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Very old memory representations might have degraded to such an extent that it is impossible to use any specific features as an efficient retrieval cue.
source: Indeed, by this time, these very old memory representations might have degraded to such an extent that it is impossible to use any specific features as an efficient retrieval cue.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of CA3 engagement.

claim: Transient inhibition of cell firing in CA1 in mice using optogenetics drastically impaired fear memory retrieval one or twenty eight days after conditioning.
source: Indeed, transient inhibition of cell firing in CA1 in mice using optogenetics drastically impaired fear memory retrieval, one or twenty eight days after conditioning (Goshen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Goshen et al., 2011.

claim: The persistent engagement of the hippocampus in memory retrieval does not involve CA3.
source: Importantly, using a high resolution molecular imaging technique, we bring the first evidence that the persistent engagement of the hippocampus in memory retrieval does not involve CA3.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on Arc expression data.

claim: Hippocampal patterns of activation observed in previous human fMRI studies investigating the retrieval of very remote memory might essentially be driven by CA1.
source: This result, in turn, suggest that hippocampal patterns of activation observed in previous human fMRI studies investigating the retrieval of very remote memory, might essentially be driven by CA1, but could not be specifically identified as such because of the limited spatial resolution of standard fMRI techniques (Ryan et al., 2001; Rekkas and Constable, 2005; Bonnici et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and limitations of fMRI.

claim: The fact that only CA1 is activated for very remote time points suggests a preferential involvement of the temporoammonic pathway over that of the trisynaptic loop for the retrieval of very remote memories.
source: Moreover, the fact that only CA1 is activated for these late time points suggests a preferential involvement of the temporoammonic pathway over that of the trisynaptic loop for the retrieval of very remote memories.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential activation of CA1 and CA3.

claim: Lesions of the temporoammonic pathway in rats specifically impaired early remote memory (28 days-old) in a Morris watermaze task, while recent memory (one day-old) was spared.
source: Robust evidence for this hypothesis is not yet available for very remote memories, but lesions of the temporoammonic pathway in rats specifically impaired early remote memory (28 days-old) in rats tested in a Morris watermaze task, while recent memory (one day-old) was spared.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Remondes and Schuman, 2004.

claim: Direct entorhinal cortex inputs to CA1 contribute to the retrieval of early remote memory, possibly by further consolidating memories.
source: This result suggests that direct entorhinal cortex inputs to CA1 contribute to the retrieval of early remote memory, possibly by further consolidating memories that were not consolidated after 28 days (Remondes and Schuman, 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited work.

claim: The temporoammonic pathway is important not only for the consolidation of memories but also for the retrieval of already consolidated memories.
source: In the present study, because we investigated a much larger time-window and found that CA1 was still activated in addition to the parahippocampal cortical areas, but not CA3, we speculate that the temporoammonic pathway is not only important for the consolidation of memories but also for the retrieval of already consolidated memories.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the current findings.

claim: The PER, the POR, the LEC and the MEC contribute to a similar extent to memory retrieval for recent and early remote time-points.
source: Our results for recent and early remote time-points match published data according to which, for example, the PER and the POR are recruited to a similar extent for contextual fear conditioning and the LEC and MEC contribute to a similar extent to memory retrieval (Bucci et al., 2002; Burwell et al., 2004; Izquierdo et al., 1997; Goshen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The contribution of the PER, the POR, the LEC and the MEC is the largest for the retrieval of very remote memories.
source: In addition, we show for the first time that the contribution of the PER, the POR, the LEC and the MEC is indeed the largest for the retrieval of very remote memories.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on Arc expression data.

claim: The amygdala sends stronger projections to the PER/LEC than to the MEC/POR.
source: Indeed, the amygdala which plays a crucial role in fear conditioning, sends stronger projections to the PER/LEC than to the MEC/POR (Pitkänen et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pitkänen et al., 2000.

claim: The differential activation of PER/LEC vs MEC/POR supports a view that parahippocampal areas might be segregated in terms of memory types/processes rather than information content.
source: Altogether, our data show a preferential role of the parahippocampal region for the retrieval of very remote memories as opposed to that of early remote and recent memories, matching the pattern commonly reported for the prefrontal cortex (Frankland and Bontempi, 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the activation patterns and anatomical connectivity.

claim: The parahippocampal region shows a preferential role for the retrieval of very remote memories as opposed to that of early remote and recent memories.
source: Altogether, our data show a preferential role of the parahippocampal region for the retrieval of very remote memories as opposed to that of early remote and recent memories, matching the pattern commonly reported for the prefrontal cortex (Frankland and Bontempi, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by Arc expression data in parahippocampal areas.

claim: The results are consistent with the view that at least the hippocampal subfield CA1 is involved in retrieving memory independently of the age of memory trace.
source: In summary, our results provide the first evidence of a disengagement of CA3 for the retrieval of very remote memories and identify CA1 as the main player at this time point. These results are consistent with the view that at least the hippocampal subfield CA1 is involved in retrieving memory independently of the age of memory trace, possibly by providing support to cortical areas that include the parahippocampal areas.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings.

claim: CA1 possibly provides support to cortical areas that include the parahippocampal areas during memory retrieval.
source: These results are consistent with the view that at least the hippocampal subfield CA1 is involved in retrieving memory independently of the age of memory trace, possibly by providing support to cortical areas that include the parahippocampal areas.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional role of CA1.

claim: Both the hippocampus and the parahippocampal region were activated independently of the age of the memory trace when CA1 and CA3 activities were averaged.
source: Of note, averaging activity levels of the hippocampal areas on the one hand and those of the parahippocampal areas on the other hand revealed that both the hippocampus and the parahippocampal region were activated independently of the age of the memory trace (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of averaged Arc expression data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The gradual transfer of the memory trace from the hippocampus to the cortex is unlikely to be an all-or-nothing phenomenon.
source: Hence, the gradual "transfer" of the memory trace from the hippocampus to the cortex is unlikely to be an all-or-nothing phenomenon, but seems to go along with a shift in the relative contribution of the two regions as the memory trace ages, and possibly a shift in the contribution of the networks they belong to.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing continued activation of both regions.

claim: The trisynaptic loop could play a preponderant role in retrieving early memories as reflected by an involvement of CA3, CA1 and the parahippocampal areas at this stage.
source: More specifically, our results suggest that the trisynaptic loop could play a preponderant role in retrieving early memories as reflected by an involvement of CA3, CA1 and the parahippocampal areas at this stage, while the retrieval of very remote memories would require an heavier contribution of the temporoamonic pathway as indicated by the lack of recruitment of CA3 and a strong activation of CA1 and the parahippocampal areas.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differential engagement patterns.

claim: The freezing index was calculated by normalizing the resting time during the first 2.5 min of test by the baseline resting time during the first 2.5 min of conditioning.

evidence: This is a methodological detail about data analysis.
